title: Te Hiku Media's te reo Māori speech recognition may be 92% accurate; archive transcription tests with the University of Auckland, RNZ and Ngā Taonga are under way
summary: Iwi broadcaster's ASR, trained on 310 hours of community recordings (86% accuracy, 2022), reported at 92% in 2024; archive tests announced in 2024 with results to come; no speaker outcome documented.
account: Te Hiku Media, a charitable iwi media and technology organization in Kaitaia, New Zealand, built its own te reo Māori automatic speech recognition. MIT Technology Review (22 April 2022) reported that a 2018 community competition collected “310 hours of speech-text pairs from some 200,000 recordings made by roughly 2,500 people” in ten days, from which, bootstrapping an open-source Mozilla model, “Te Hiku created its very first te reo speech recognition model with 86% accuracy”; the tools are offered through the Papa Reo platform. NVIDIA's blog (16 January 2024) says the model “transcribes te reo Māori with 92% accuracy” using the NeMo toolkit, and an RNZ release of 11 September 2024 quotes Te Hiku chief executive Peter-Lucas Jones in te reo giving the same 92% figure. The University of Auckland announced on 18 March 2024, the date used here, that its Archive of Māori and Pacific Sound is collaborating with Te Hiku Media to test the tool on archival recordings with different dialects, recording qualities and sung forms, comparing automatic output “against human-generated ones”, with results to be shared with the galleries, libraries, archives and museums sector; it says the tool “is performing very well for their purposes” in Te Hiku's broadcasting arm. RNZ and Ngā Taonga Sound & Vision agreed in September 2024 to supply previously broadcast te reo recordings to train and review the tools. No source on file reports a measured outcome for a speaker, learner or archive user; the accuracy figures originate with Te Hiku Media and NVIDIA.
purpose: Built to transcribe te reo Māori recordings so that archives and broadcasts become searchable and readable by learners, under Māori data-sovereignty rules; the transcription tests are that intended use.
system: Te Hiku Media te reo Māori automatic speech recognition and transcription tool (Papa Reo platform; trained with Mozilla DeepSpeech-era open-source tooling, later NVIDIA NeMo)
deployer: Te Hiku Media broadcasting arm; test partners Archive of Māori and Pacific Sound (University of Auckland), RNZ and Ngā Taonga Sound & Vision
taxonomy_note: The documented good is recognition accuracy; serving te reo Maori speakers would be inclusion, but no speaker outcome is reported.

ratings.reason: Te Hiku Media and its archive partners report the tool performs well for broadcasting and are testing it on archival material; no measured time saving or completed archive transcription is documented.
Benefits to te reo speakers and learners are the stated aim; no source on file measures them.

ai_role.statement: The accuracy figures come from Te Hiku Media (86% reported by MIT Technology Review in 2022; 92% stated by NVIDIA, a tooling vendor, and by Te Hiku's chief executive through RNZ in 2024). The University of Auckland's independent test compares outputs against human transcripts with results to follow; no source on file reports an outcome for any speaker, learner or archive beyond the developer's own broadcasting use.

produced_by: A community-contributed read-speech corpus (310 hours in ten days) held under Te Hiku Media's data-sovereignty rules
Bootstrapping from open-source speech models and, later, NVIDIA's NeMo toolkit
must_hold: Recordings resemble the training data; the 2024 tests deliberately probe regional dialects, recording quality and sung forms such as mōteatea and waiata
Archive holders license recordings on the partners' conditions (no pecuniary gain, previously broadcast material only)

echoes.setting: RNZ and Ngā Taonga archive-access agreement to train and review the tools on historical te reo broadcasts

headline: Te Hiku Media's te reo Māori recognition may be 92% accurate
metric: transcribes te reo Māori with 92% accuracy

comparator.against: te reo Māori speech recognition attempts by major tech companies
comparator.quote: Our tools already outperform attempts by major tech companies at te reo Māori ASR, with an accuracy of 92%.

later.note: RNZ announced on 11 September 2024 that it is integrating Te Hiku's Papa Reo API into its workflows for search and captions, with RNZ and Ngā Taonga supplying archival te reo broadcasts to train and review the tools.
later.quote: RNZ is in the process of integrating the Papa Reo API into its workflows, initially adding transcribed audio to the search capability and then allowing it to add captions to its player in the near future.
